title: Rare events and the zero-hit bound
observe: With p = 0.0002 and 8,192 replicates, the run often shows 0, 1 or 2 hits. After 0 hits, the CLT interval is the point 0, and it does not contain p. The exact zero-hit bound 1 − 0.05^(1/n), about 3/n, stays valid. Increase the number of replicates n. Then the width of the Wilson interval decreases.

problem: How many draws show a rare event, and what does a run with no hits tell?
param p = 0.0002 "probability of the event in one draw"

prob hit = X == 1 "probability of the event"

title: A third server or a second power feed?
decision: Decision: install a third server, or a second power feed. Estimated quantity: the daily outage probability θ = P(down = 1) for each alternative.
reason: On one day, each fault either occurs or does not, so each fault is a Bernoulli variable. A common power fault C stops all servers at once. This is the shared-cause idea of the beta-factor model in reliability work.
inputs: pc = 0.0005 and pf = 0.01 per day are illustrative values. The unit is a probability for each day. There is no data. The model assumes identical, independent days.
dependence: C acts on every server. Given C = 0, the faults A, B and T are independent. Thus all dependence comes from the one shared cause.
method: Independent draws of the 4 indicators in each replicate. The estimator is the fraction of replicates with an outage. All alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences usually have a smaller variance than with independent streams.
diagnostics: The Wilson interval, and the exact zero-hit bound when a run has no outage. The enumeration of the 16 joint states gives the exact reference. Other candidate models: fault times with repair times, and server faults that depend on the load.
interpretation: The second power feed lowers the outage probability most, because the common fault dominates. A third server acts only on the small term pf². It does not change the larger term pc. Reject the model if outages cluster on consecutive days, or if server faults correlate without a power fault.

param pf = 0.01 "daily probability of an independent fault of one server"
param third = 0 "1 when a third server is installed"

B ~ bernoulli(p = pf) "fault of server B"

title: Screen, treat everyone, or treat no one?
decision: Decision: treat after a positive test, treat everyone, or treat no one. Estimated quantity: the expected cost for each person, and the probability of disease after a positive test.
reason: A person has the disease or not, and a test is positive or not. Both are Bernoulli variables. The test result depends on the disease state through the sensitivity and the specificity.
inputs: Prevalence 0.02, sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.95 are illustrative values. Costs are in cost units: 1 for one treatment, 40 for one untreated case. There is no data.
dependence: T depends on D: P(T = 1 | D = 1) = sens and P(T = 1 | D = 0) = 1 − spec. Different people are independent.
method: Independent draws of D, then of T given D. The cost estimator is a sample mean. The probability of disease after a positive test is a ratio of 2 means, with a delta-method interval.
diagnostics: CLT intervals for the costs, which have finite bounds. The paired differences compare the policies on the same people. Other candidate models: a prevalence with its own uncertainty, and test errors that depend on the stage of the disease.
interpretation: With these values, the policy that treats after a positive test costs about 0.15 cost units for each person. No treatment costs 0.8, and treatment of everyone costs 1. Only about 27 % of positive tests come from a person with the disease. Reject the model if the sensitivity or the specificity differs between groups of patients.

title: Screen, treat everyone, or treat no one?
problem: A test detects a disease with errors. Find the policy with the least expected cost for each person.
param prev = 0.02 "prevalence of the disease"
param sens = 0.9 "probability of a positive test for a person with the disease"
param spec = 0.95 "probability of a negative test for a person without the disease"
param ctreat = 1 {cost units} "cost of one treatment"
param cmiss = 40 {cost units} "cost of one untreated case"
param policy = 1 "1 = treat when positive, 2 = treat all, 3 = treat none"
D ~ bernoulli(p = prev) "the person has the disease"
T ~ bernoulli(p = if(D, sens, 1 - spec)) "the test is positive"

alt "Treat everyone": policy = 2
alt "Treat no one": policy = 3
minimise cost
focus T

title: The vote threshold of a launch abort system
decision: Decision: the number k of sensor alarms that starts an abort. Estimated quantity: the expected cost for each launch, with the probabilities of a false abort and of a missed fault.
reason: Each sensor alarm and the fault itself are Bernoulli variables. Given the fault state, each sensor alarms with a fixed probability.
inputs: P(fault) = 0.001, P(alarm | fault) = 0.95 and P(alarm | no fault) = 0.02 are illustrative values. Costs: 1 cost unit for an abort without a fault, 500 for a launch that continues with a fault.
dependence: The 3 alarms are independent given Fault. They are dependent without that condition, because all of them follow Fault.
method: Independent draws of Fault, then of S1, S2 and S3 given Fault. The cost estimator is a sample mean. The 3 alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: The enumeration of the 16 joint states gives exact reference values. The missed-fault probability is rare, so the zero-hit bound matters for a small number of replicates. Other candidate model: a common-mode sensor error, which makes the alarms dependent given Fault.
interpretation: k = 2 gives the least expected cost. k = 1 aborts too often, and k = 3 misses too many faults. A run needs about 10^6 replicates, because a missed fault with k = 2 has a probability near 7 in a million. A smaller run often shows no missed fault, and its cost estimate is then too low. Reject the model if the sensors share a power supply or a software fault.

dependence: None in this model: ticket holders are independent. Groups that travel together break this assumption.
method: The inverse transform or independent draws of X. The estimators are sample means. The alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences usually have a smaller variance than with independent streams.
diagnostics: Exact reference values by enumeration of the 193 support points. The constraint P(any passenger loses the seat) ≤ 0.05 uses the interval, not only the estimate. Other candidate models: the beta-binomial law for groups, and a show probability that depends on the fare class.
interpretation: 186 tickets give more revenue than 180, and they meet the constraint. 192 tickets do not meet the constraint. Reject the model if many passengers travel in groups, because the variance of X is then larger.

title: An inspection plan for parts from a supplier

reason: A large lot holds many parts, so each sampled part has a defect independently with the lot fraction. Thus the number of parts with a defect in the sample has a law near the binomial law.
inputs: The acceptable quality level 1 % and the limit 8 % are illustrative values. The unit of X is parts with a defect. There is no data.
dependence: None: parts are independent within the sample. The binomial law replaces the hypergeometric law, which is exact for a finite lot.
method: Independent draws of the 2 counts. Each estimator is a fraction of replicates. Sweep nsample or c to see how the probabilities of acceptance change.
diagnostics: The page checks each risk constraint against the interval. Exact references come from the enumeration. Other candidate model: the hypergeometric law for a small lot.
interpretation: No plan with nsample = 50 meets both limits. With c = 1, the plan rejects 8.9 % of good lots. With c = 2, it accepts 22.6 % of bad lots. The plan nsample = 100, c = 3 meets both limits. Reject the binomial model if the sample is more than about 10 % of the lot.

title: Are Weldon's dice fair?
decision: Decision: keep or reject the fair-dice model for Weldon's dice. Estimated quantity: P(X ≥ 7), the probability of 7 or more dice with 5 or 6, under the fair model and under the fitted model.
reason: One throw of 12 dice gives 12 trials. Each die shows 5 or 6 with probability 1/3 if it is fair. Thus the count of such dice is Binomial(12, p).
inputs: Real data: 26,306 throws, with the counts of dice that show 5 or 6. The fitted p is the maximum likelihood estimate, the mean count divided by 12. The unit of X is dice.
dependence: None in the model: dice and throws are independent. A die with a bias affects every throw, so it changes p and not the independence.
method: Independent draws of X under each alternative. The estimator of P(X ≥ 7) is a fraction of replicates. The data panel compares the observed counts with the expected counts.
diagnostics: The chi-square test of the data against Binomial(12, 1/3) and against the fitted law, with pooled cells. Other candidate model: different values of p for different dice. That model gives the same mean count but a different variance.
interpretation: The fair model fails the chi-square test, and the fitted p = 0.3377 passes it. Dice that show 5 or 6 a little more often than 1/3 explain the data. Do not read the fitted p as the bias of one die, because the data mix 12 dice. Reject the binomial model if the counts spread less than a binomial law allows, because dice with different p give a smaller variance. Also reject it if the counts spread more, because p then changes between throws.

title: Are Weldon's dice fair?
problem: W. F. R. Weldon threw 12 dice 26,306 times and counted the dice that showed 5 or 6. Find whether the fair-dice model explains the counts.
param ndice = 12 {dice}
param p = 1/3 "probability that one die shows 5 or 6"
X ~ binomial(n = ndice, p = p) {dice that show 5 or 6}
prob seven_plus = X >= 7 "7 or more dice show 5 or 6"
mean average = X {dice} "mean count"
alt "Fair dice": p = 1/3
alt "Fitted p = 0.3377": p = 0.3377
focus X

dependence: The stay depends on the level: H | L ~ Poisson(stay_L). Arrivals are independent.
method: Independent draws: the alias method for L, then a Poisson draw for H. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates.
diagnostics: Exact reference values by enumeration of the level and the stay. Other candidate model: a continuous stay with a gamma law, or with a lognormal law (group 3). The Poisson count of hours has a variance equal to its mean, which can be too small for real stays.
interpretation: With these values, about 5 % of arrivals stay over 8 hours, so the department does not need the unit. Reject the Poisson stay model if the variance of the stay in one level is larger than its mean.

diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration of the 5 outcomes. The paired difference between the alternatives uses the same streams. Other candidate model: one order with several returned items, with a multinomial count for each order.

title: Do genotype counts depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions?
decision: Decision: flag the sample for a departure from Hardy–Weinberg proportions if the p-value is below 0.05. Estimated quantity: the Monte Carlo p-value P(T ≥ t_obs) of the chi-square statistic T.
reason: Under the null model, each person has genotype AA, Aa or aa with the Hardy–Weinberg probabilities (q², 2q(1 − q), (1 − q)²). Thus the genotype counts are multinomial.
inputs: Synthetic counts AA = 58, Aa = 84, aa = 58 from 200 people. The allele frequency estimate is q = 0.5, and the observed statistic is t_obs = 5.12.
dependence: None: the people have no family relation. The counts share the total n.
method: Independent draws of the counts under the null model with q = 0.5. In each replicate, a new estimate of q replaces the true q, as for the observed statistic. The p-value estimator is the fraction of replicates with T ≥ t_obs. This is a parametric bootstrap.
diagnostics: An enumeration of all 20,301 outcomes gives the exact p-value of this bootstrap. The chi-square law with 1 degree of freedom gives 0.024. A version that keeps q fixed gives about 0.08, near the chi-square law with 2 degrees of freedom, because it ignores the estimation of q. Other candidate method: the exact test that conditions on the allele counts (Wigginton, Cutler and Abecasis 2005).
interpretation: The p-value is near 0.025, so the page flags the sample. The sample has 84 heterozygotes, against 100 under the model. title: A die that protects survey answers
decision: Decision: the number t of die faces on which a respondent answers the sensitive question truthfully. Estimated quantity: the probability that the estimate of the share π is within 0.05, and the disclosure risk P(trait | yes).

reason: The auditors take n ballots without replacement from a batch of N, of which K are misread. The count of misread ballots found is hypergeometric.
inputs: A batch of 500 ballots with 10 misread ballots is an illustrative case. There is no data.
dependence: None: the audit draws a simple random sample of ballots.
method: Inverse transform from the mode. A binomial count Y with p = K/N shows the error of the binomial approximation.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate model: the binomial approximation Y. It gives a slightly smaller probability, because draws with replacement can repeat a ballot.
interpretation: 150 ballots find a misread ballot with a probability above 0.9. 100 ballots give about 0.89, just below the target. Reject the model if the misread ballots cluster in one part of the batch and the sample is not random.

dsl:
title: How many ballots to audit in a batch?
problem: A batch of 500 paper ballots may hold 10 misread ballots. An audit checks n ballots by hand. Find n so that the audit finds at least one misread ballot.
param N = 500 {ballots}
param K = 10 {ballots} "misread ballots in the batch"
param n = 100 {ballots} "ballots checked by hand"
X ~ hypergeometric(N = N, K = K, n = n) {misread ballots found}
Y ~ binomial(n = n, p = K / N) {misread ballots found} "the binomial approximation"
prob found = X >= 1 "the audit finds a misread ballot"
prob found_binomial = Y >= 1 "the same probability under the binomial approximation"
alt "n = 50": n = 50
alt "n = 100": n = 100
alt "n = 150": n = 150
require found >= 0.9
focus X

title: How many lands in a 60-card deck?
decision: Decision: the number of land cards in a 60-card deck. Estimated quantity: the probability of a first hand of 7 cards with 2 to 4 lands. At most 10 % of hands can have 5 or more lands.
reason: A shuffled deck gives a hand of 7 cards without replacement. The count of lands in the hand is hypergeometric.
inputs: Deck size 60 and hand size 7 are game rules. The land counts 22, 24 and 26 are the alternatives.
dependence: None: a fair shuffle gives every hand the same probability.
method: Urn simulation of 7 draws, or the inverse transform. The estimators are fractions of replicates.
diagnostics: Exact references by enumeration. Other candidate model: a rule that lets a player draw a new hand, which changes the law of the kept hand.
interpretation: 26 lands give the highest probability of a hand with 2 to 4 lands, 0.78, but too many hands with 5 or more lands. 24 lands give almost the same value, 0.77, and meet the limit. Reject the model if the players do not shuffle the deck well.

title: An infinite mean stops the law of large numbers
observe: For the zeta law with s = 1.8, E[X] is infinite. The sample mean tends to ∞, so it has no finite limit. It increases in a step each time a very large rank appears. The page shows no interval and no reference value, because no finite mean exists.

title: How large should a web cache be?
decision: Decision: the number C of pages in the cache. Estimated quantity: the hit ratio, the probability that a request finds its page in the cache.
reason: The popularity of a page often falls with its rank as a power law. A Zipf law with exponent near 1 is a standard model of web requests.
inputs: 10,000 pages and the exponent s = 0.9 are illustrative values. The cache holds the C most popular pages.
dependence: None: requests are independent. Real requests show bursts of repeated pages, which help a cache.
method: Inverse transform with a CDF table. The estimator is the fraction of requests with X ≤ C.
diagnostics: Exact references: H(C, s)/H(N, s). Other candidate model: popularity that changes over time, which needs a cache that adapts.
interpretation: 1,000 pages give a hit ratio near 0.67 and meet the target 0.6. 500 pages give about 0.59. Reject the model if the exponent varies between days, because the hit ratio depends strongly on s.

title: How large must the dictionary of a spell checker be?
decision: Decision: the number D of words in the dictionary of a spell checker. Estimated quantity: the probability that a message of 300 words holds more than 30 words outside the dictionary.
reason: Word frequencies in text fall with rank roughly as a power law with exponent near 1 (Zipf's law of word frequencies).
inputs: A vocabulary of 50,000 ranks and the exponent s = 1.1 are illustrative values. A message has 300 words.
dependence: This model draws the 300 words independently. In real text, words repeat and follow topics, so the words are not independent.
method: Inverse transform with a CDF table for each of the 300 words. The estimator is a fraction of messages.
diagnostics: No enumeration: each message has 300 variables. Other candidate model: a topic model in which the rank law changes from message to message.
interpretation: Only the dictionary of 20,000 words keeps messages with more than 30 unknown words below 5 %. Even then a message holds about 14 unknown words, because the Zipf tail is long. Reject the independence assumption for long texts, where words repeat.

title: Server capacity for viral posts
decision: Decision: plan capacity for posts with more than 10,000 shares. Estimated quantity: P(X > 10,000) for one post, and the mean number of shares.
reason: Share counts of posts have a power-law tail. The zeta law is the discrete law with P(X = k) proportional to k^(−s) on all positive integers.
inputs: The tail exponents s = 2.3 and s = 2.1 are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None: posts are independent in this model. Real shares spread through a network, which the branching processes of the process group describe.
method: Rejection from a Pareto proposal (Devroye). The tail probability estimator is a fraction of replicates. The mean estimator is a sample mean.
diagnostics: The mean is finite for s > 2, but the variance is infinite for s ≤ 3. Thus the page gives no CLT interval for the mean. The tail probability has an exact reference from the Hurwitz zeta function. Other candidate model: a lognormal law, which has all moments.
interpretation: About 3 in a million posts pass 10,000 shares when s = 2.3. A small change of s changes this probability several times. Plan from the tail probability and its sensitivity to s, not from the mean. Reject the model if the real counts have a tail that decays faster.

title: Monte Carlo integration of a quarter circle
observe: The estimate of area is near the reference π/4 ≈ 0.7854 from quadrature, and low is near 0.3. The interval of area has a width of about 0.014 with 4,096 replicates, 0.0069 with 16,384 and 0.0034 with 65,536. So 4 times more replicates halve the width, because the standard error falls as 1/√n. The height sqrt(1 − U²) is smooth and decreases in U, so both stratification and antithetic pairs help. title: Which transit line takes a rider to work in the least time?
decision: Decision: the line that a rider takes to work. Estimated quantity: the mean time from the arrival at the stop to the destination, and the probability that the rider is late.
reason: The vehicles of one line leave the stop at a fixed headway. The rider comes to the stop at a time that has no relation to the timetable. The wait until the next vehicle is then uniform between 0 and the headway.
inputs: Headways of 12, 6 and 20 min and ride times of 22, 26 and 16 min are illustrative values. The rider has 33 min before the start of work. There is no data.
dependence: None between the wait and the ride: the ride time is a constant of each line. The model also ignores delays on the road, which would add a second random time.
method: Independent draws of the wait W = headway · U, with U uniform on (0, 1). The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. The alternatives use common random numbers, so one U gives the wait on each line. For the mean time, the variance ratio against independent alternatives is 5 (tram − bus), 8.5 (express − bus) and 2.2 (express − tram). With separate streams each ratio is near 1.
diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact mean time headway/2 + ride: 28, 29 and 26 min. Quadrature gives P(late): 1/12 ≈ 0.083 for the bus, 0 for the tram and 0.15 for the express. Other candidate models: an exponential wait for a line with random departures, and a longer mean wait E[H](1 + CV²)/2 when the headways H vary.
interpretation: The bus has the least mean time among the lines that meet the constraint: about 28.0 min, against 29.0 min for the tram. The express is faster, about 26.0 min, but the rider is late with P(late) ≈ 0.15, above the limit 0.1. The paired intervals separate the bus from the tram. Reject the model if the vehicles come in groups or the rider follows a timetable, because the wait is then not uniform.

title: Round each invoice line or only the total?
decision: Decision: the rule that rounds the amounts of a 30-line invoice. Estimated quantity: the probability that the buyer rejects the invoice, the mean absolute error of the total, and the mean cost for each invoice.
reason: Each line amount has digits below the rounding step. Prices and quantities vary, so the part below one step is close to uniform. The error of one rounded line is then uniform between −0.5 and +0.5 steps, independently of the other lines.
inputs: The model uses illustrative values: 30 lines and a tolerance of 1 cent in the buyer's match. A rejected invoice costs 12 currency units of manual work. The new layouts cost 0.02 and 0.05 currency units for each invoice. There is no data.
dependence: None: the errors of different lines are independent. Lines that repeat one price, such as many units of one item at a price with 3 decimals, break this assumption.
method: Independent draws of the 30 line errors and of the error of the total, each by a scaled uniform. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. For the first rule, the total error is a sum of 30 uniform values. Its law is the Irwin–Hall law, moved to the mean 0.
diagnostics: The page shows no reference values: the line errors are a repeated variable, and the quadrature does not integrate over 30 copies. For the sum S of 30 line errors, the Irwin–Hall law gives P(|S| > 1) = 0.5289 exactly. The CLT gives about 0.527. Other candidate models: a discrete error on a grid of 0.1 cent, and dependent errors for lines that repeat one price.
interpretation: Round each line fails the constraint: about 53 % of the invoices differ from the buyer's total by more than 1 cent. Its mean absolute error is about 1.26 cents. The page selects Lines to 0.1 cent, with the least mean cost: about 0.021 against 0.05 currency units for Round only the total. Its P(reject) is about 7 × 10⁻⁵. Reject the model if many lines repeat one price, because the errors are then dependent and not uniform.

title: Which tolerance class fits a shaft to its hole at the least cost?
decision: Decision: the tolerance class of a shaft and its hole. Estimated quantity: the probability that the clearance is outside the functional range, and the mean cost for each pair of parts.
reason: Tool wear moves each diameter at a constant rate between two tool changes, from one end of its band to the other. A part made at a random time then has a uniform diameter on its band.
inputs: The nominal diameter is 20 mm. The bands follow the ISO 286 grades for 18 to 30 mm: IT8 = 33 µm, IT7 = 21 µm, IT6 = 13 µm and IT5 = 9 µm. The shaft band starts 7 µm below the nominal size. The functional range of 8 to 38 µm and all costs are illustrative values. There is no data.
dependence: None: the hole and the shaft come from different machines, so their diameters are independent. Selective assembly, which pairs large shafts with large holes, breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of H and S by scaled uniforms. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. The alternatives use common random numbers, but each class scales the uniforms in a different way. So the variance ratio against independent alternatives stays between 0.99 and 1.2.
diagnostics: Quadrature over the 2 uniform variables gives the reference values. P(misfit) is 0.3795, 0.0183 and 0.0043, and the mean cost is 12.89, 2.55 and 3.03 currency units. The clearance H − S has a trapezoidal law, so these values also have a closed form. Other candidate models: a normal law cut to each band for a centred process, and a triangular law for a process with little tool wear.
interpretation: The fine class IT6/IT5 is the only class that meets the constraint. Its P(misfit) is about 0.004, and its mean cost is about 3.03 currency units. The medium class costs less, about 2.55, but its P(misfit) of about 0.018 is above the limit 0.01. The coarse class scraps about 38 % of the pairs. Reject the model if the diameters gather near the centre of each band, because the misfit probabilities are then smaller.

title: The normal law and the 68–95–99.7 rule
observe: The estimates of upper and two_sided are near their references 0.1587 and 0.0455, and sq_dev is near σ² = 4. By symmetry, P(|X − μ| ≤ σ) = 1 − 2 × 0.1587 ≈ 0.683 and P(|X − μ| ≤ 2σ) ≈ 0.954. With 3σ the value is 0.997, so the rule reads 68–95–99.7 %. With antithetic variables, the variance ratio of two_sided and sq_dev is 0.50, a loss, and the ratio of upper is about 1.23. The partner X' = 2μ − X gives the same value of an even function of X − μ. So a pair costs 2 evaluations for the information of 1.

title: How many loaves to bake for one day?
decision: Decision: the number of loaves to bake each morning. Estimated quantity: the mean profit for each day, and the probability that the demand is above the stock.
reason: The daily demand is the sum of the purchases of many customers who act independently. By the CLT, such a sum is close to normal when the mean count is large, here 400 loaves.
inputs: The mean demand of 400 loaves and its standard deviation of 80 loaves are illustrative values. So are the price of 3 and the cost of 1 currency unit for each loaf. Unsold loaves have no value. P(D < 0) = Φ(−5) ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁷ is negligible, and the model uses max(D, 0). There is no data.
dependence: None: the model looks at one day. Weather and the day of the week change the mean demand. A separate model for each type of day removes that dependence.
method: Independent draws of D. The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. The control C = D has the exact mean 400. With control variates, the variance ratio of profit is about 3.8 for 400 loaves, 7.4 for 440 and 17 for 480. The ratio is large because profit has a strong correlation with D. With the failure control_mean, the control mean is wrong by 0.1σ, and the estimates move 12 to 20 currency units above their references.
diagnostics: Quadrature over D gives the reference values: mean profit 704.25, 712.53 and 700.00, and P(short) = 0.5, 0.3085 and 0.1587. The closed form E[min(D, q)] = μ − σ[φ(z) − z(1 − Φ(z))], with z = (q − μ)/σ, gives the same values. With the failure control_mean, the estimates are 41 to 105 standard errors from their references at 2^16 replicates. Other candidate models: a negative binomial count for a small bakery, and a gamma demand with a long right tail.
interpretation: Without the constraint, 440 loaves give the largest mean profit, about 712.5 against 704.3 for 400 and 700.0 for 480. The constraint P(short) ≤ 0.25 removes 400 and 440 loaves, so the page selects 480 loaves. The constraint costs about 12.5 currency units of mean profit each day. Reject the model if the sales data show a skewed demand. Reject it also if many days end with an empty shelf, because the stock then cuts the observed demand.

title: Does a stack of three parts fit its housing?
decision: Decision: a standard or a precision part C in a stack of three parts. Estimated quantity: the probability that the stack is longer than the housing gap, the mean slack, and the mean cost for each assembly.
reason: Each length is the result of many small independent effects of the machine, the tool and the material. By the CLT, each length is close to normal. The stack length is a sum of independent normal lengths, so it is also normal.
inputs: These values are illustrative: mean lengths of 20, 30 and 50 mm, and a gap of 100.15 mm. The standard deviations are σ_A = σ_B = 0.02 mm, and σ_C = 0.08 mm or 0.03 mm for the precision part. The precision part costs 1.2 currency units more, and one assembly that does not fit costs 30 currency units. There is no data.
dependence: None: the three parts come from different processes. Parts from one batch with the same tool offset have correlated lengths, and the stack variance is then larger.
method: Independent draws of A, B and C. The estimators are fractions and means of replicates. Stratification helps only on the variable that drives the variance. With 16 strata of A, the variance ratio for the standard part is about 1.01 for no_fit and 1.06 for slack. A gives only 5.6 % of the stack variance. With 16 strata of C, which gives 89 %, the ratios are about 1.8 and 7.6.
diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact reference of the mean slack, 0.15 mm. The page has no reference for no_fit and cost, because the model has 3 continuous variables. For a sum of independent normal values, P(no_fit) = 1 − Φ(0.15/√0.0072) = 0.0385 for the standard part. For the precision part it is 1.4 × 10⁻⁴. Other candidate models: a worst-case stack of the tolerance limits, and a uniform law for parts from a process with tool wear.
interpretation: The standard part C fails the constraint: about 3.9 % of the assemblies do not fit. Its mean cost, about 1.16, is close to the 1.20 of the precision part. The precision part meets the constraint with P(no_fit) of about 0.00014, so the page selects it. Reject the model if the lengths of part C have heavier tails than a normal law, because the misfit rate then grows.

title: Cold drinks or hot drinks at a summer festival?
decision: Decision: the type of drinks stall to rent for a one-day festival. Estimated quantity: the mean profit of the day, and the probability of a loss.
reason: The maximum temperature T of the day is the forecast value plus a forecast error. The error of a forecast one or two days ahead is close to normal, so T is normal around the forecast.
inputs: These values are illustrative: a forecast of 22 °C with a standard deviation of 3 °C, and a stall fee of 600 currency units. Cold drinks sell 900 at 20 °C and 80 more for each °C above. Hot drinks sell 1000 at 20 °C and 60 less for each °C above. There is no data.
dependence: None: the model looks at one day, and the profit is a linear function of T. Sales that stop at the capacity of the stall break the linear form.
method: Independent draws of T. The estimators are means and fractions of replicates. Common random numbers fail here: the cold profit rises with T and the hot profit falls, so their covariance is negative. The variance ratio against independent alternatives for the profit difference is 0.51, a loss. With separate streams it is near 1.
diagnostics: Linearity gives the exact mean profit: 300 + 80 × 2 = 460 for cold drinks and 400 − 60 × 2 = 280 for hot drinks. Quadrature gives P(loss) = Φ((16.25 − 22)/3) = 0.0276 and 1 − Φ((26.67 − 22)/3) = 0.0599. Other candidate models: a forecast error with heavier tails, such as a Student t law, and sales that stop at the capacity of the stall.

title: Which asset mix gives the best mean return with a limited loss risk?
decision: Decision: the weights of bonds, equities and property in a fund. Estimated quantity: the mean monthly return, and the probability of a monthly loss worse than 4 %.
reason: A monthly return is the sum of many small price changes, so a normal law is a common first model. The three assets react to the same economic news, so their returns are correlated. The multivariate normal law holds the means, the volatilities and the correlations in one covariance matrix.
inputs: The monthly means are 0.3, 0.8 and 0.6 % for bonds, equities and property, and the standard deviations are 1, 4.5 and 3.5 %. The correlations are −0.2 for bonds and equities, 0.1 for bonds and property, and 0.6 for equities and property. These values are illustrative, not market estimates. The loss limit is 4 % in one month.
dependence: The covariance matrix holds the dependence: [1, −0.9, 0.35; −0.9, 20.25, 9.45; 0.35, 9.45, 12.25] in %². The months are independent in this model. The normal law has no tail dependence, so in this model large losses do not come together more often than the correlations say.
method: Independent draws: R = μ + LZ, with L the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix and Z a vector of standard normal values. The estimators are a sample mean and a fraction of replicates. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences of the mean return are precise.
diagnostics: The mean return has an exact reference by linearity: 0.43, 0.56 and 0.69 % a month. The loss probability has no reference on the page, because the page does not integrate over a vector law. The fund return is normal with a mean m and a standard deviation s. So Φ((−4 − m)/s) gives a check: about 0.0002, 0.022 and 0.085. Other candidate models: a multivariate Student t law for heavy tails, and a t copula for losses that come together.
interpretation: The growth mix has the largest mean, 0.69 % a month. But its probability of a loss worse than 4 % is about 0.085, above the limit 0.05. The balanced mix meets the limit with about 0.022, and its mean 0.56 % is the best of the admissible mixes. Reject the model if the returns show heavy tails, or if large losses come together more often than the normal law allows.

title: Which z-score rule should flag a child for a growth review?
decision: Decision: the z-score rule that flags a child for a growth review. Estimated quantity: the false-flag rate among healthy children, and the detection rate among children with a growth disorder.
reason: Growth references define the height and weight z-scores so that they are close to standard normal in healthy children. Tall children are also heavier, so the two z-scores are correlated. A bivariate normal law keeps both margins and the correlation.
inputs: The correlation 0.65 and the flag limit −2 are illustrative values. So are the mean z-scores with the disorder: −1.5 for height and −1.0 for weight. Both groups have the same covariance. The clinic accepts a false-flag rate of at most 0.03.
dependence: The covariance matrix [1, 0.65; 0.65, 1] holds the dependence of the two z-scores of one child. Each replicate draws one healthy child and one child with the disorder, independently.
method: Independent draws: μ + LZ with the Cholesky factor L of the covariance matrix. The estimators are fractions of replicates. All rules read the same draws, so the differences between the rules are paired.
diagnostics: No reference value: the page does not integrate over a vector law. A check: the height rule flags Φ(−2) ≈ 0.0228 of healthy children. With independent z-scores, the either rule would flag 0.045 and the both rule 0.0005. The correlation 0.65 gives about 0.039 and 0.0064. Other candidate models: a skewed law for the weight z-score, and a mixture with an unknown share of children with the disorder.
interpretation: The either rule detects the most, about 0.35, but it flags about 0.039 of healthy children, above 0.03. The height rule flags about 0.023 and detects about 0.31. The both rule detects only about 0.12. So the height rule is the best admissible rule. Reject the model if the z-scores of the local population are not near standard normal, or if the correlation differs much from 0.65.

reason: Each sensor error is the sum of many small effects, so a normal law fits. The two sensors share some effects, such as the same atmospheric delay or the same map error, so their errors are correlated. A bivariate normal law describes this pair of errors.
inputs: Error standard deviations of 2 m and 3 m, a correlation of 0.5 and an error limit of 4 m are illustrative values. Both sensors have no bias. The combined estimate must have P(|error| > 4 m) of at most 0.05.

title: Which timeout for a call to a slow service?
decision: Decision: the timeout of a web page for its call to a service. Estimated quantity: the probability of a timeout, the mean user wait, and the expected cost of the wait and the cached results.
reason: The service works as a single queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times. In such a queue the response time is exponential. The law has no memory. A request that has waited 400 ms has the same law for the rest of its wait as a new request. So a timeout helps only against the requests that the service loses.
inputs: A mean response time of 250 ms and a loss probability of 0.02 are illustrative values. So is the cost of a cached result, equal to 2000 ms of user wait. The latency target is a wait of at most 1.5 s in 99 % of page views.

A 2000 ms timeout has the least cost, about 326 ms, but 2.2 % of page views wait more than 1.5 s. The 1000 ms timeout meets the target with a cost of about 336 ms. title: Which deductible and cap to offer on a home contents contract

method: Independent draws by the Marsaglia–Tsang method. The estimators are sample means and a fraction. The payout is monotone in L, so the antithetic pairs U and 1 − U give negatively correlated payouts. With the antithetic method, the variance ratio of the mean payout is about 14, 5 and 3 for the three contracts. The control C = L, with the exact mean 5000, gives variance ratios between about 11 and 100.

Of the admissible contracts, the deductible 2000 with the cap 20000 gives the larger margin, 659 against 613. Reject the model if large claims are more frequent than the gamma tail allows, because the model then understates P(payout at the cap).

title: Which repair-time guarantee to sell in a service contract

method: Independent draws by the Marsaglia–Tsang method. The estimators are a fraction and sample means of quantities with finite moments. The alternatives use the same draws, so the paired differences are precise.
diagnostics: Quadrature reference values for every quantity. P(late) is 0.186, 0.075 and 0.029, and the expected margin is 287.1, 247.1 and 200.2. Other candidate models: a log-normal repair time, and a mixture for the calls that wait for parts.

title: How many cold spare boards for a remote relay station
decision: Decision: the number of control boards that a remote relay station keeps as cold spares. Estimated quantity: the probability that the station works until the next service visit, and the expected cost of the boards and of a failure.
reason: A board in use fails at a constant rate, so its life is exponential. A cold spare does not age while it is off, and the switch is perfect. The station life is then the sum of k i.i.d. exponential lives: the Erlang(k, λ) law.
inputs: A failure rate of 0.0005 an hour gives a mean board life of 2000 hours. This rate, the 3000 hours to the next visit and the costs are illustrative values. A board costs 40 thousand currency units, and a station failure costs 500 thousand. The operator needs a survival probability of at least 0.9.
dependence: None: the board lives are independent. A switch that can fail, or spares that age while they are off, break the Erlang model.
method: Independent draws as the sum of k exponential phases: X = −Σ log(U_i)/λ. The estimators are a fraction and sample means. The alternatives use the same streams, so the paired differences are precise.
diagnostics: Exact references for P(survive) and E[T] = k/λ from the Erlang law, and a quadrature reference for the cost. P(survive) = P(N < k) for a Poisson count N with the mean λt = 1.5: 0.809, 0.934 and 0.981. Other candidate models: a warm standby with spares that age at a lower rate, and an imperfect switch.
interpretation: 2 spares give a survival probability of about 0.81, below 0.9. 3 spares meet the target with 0.934 and give the least expected cost, about 192.8 thousand. 4 spares give an expected cost of 209.3 thousand, because the extra board costs more than the risk it removes. Reject the model if the failure rate grows with age, or if the switch can fail.

title: When to call a second doctor to the emergency department at night
decision: Decision: the number k of patients in 30 minutes that calls a second doctor to the emergency department at night. Estimated quantity: the probability of a call, the call rates on normal and surge nights, and the expected cost for each night.
reason: Patients arrive independently at a constant rate during the night, so the arrivals form a Poisson process. The time of the k-th arrival is then the sum of k exponential gaps: the Erlang(k, λ) law. The rate is higher on a surge night.
inputs: The arrival rates of 3 patients an hour on a normal night and 8 on a surge night are illustrative values. So are the surge probability 0.2, the call cost 400 and the cost 2000 of a surge night with one doctor. The window is the first 30 minutes of the night shift.
dependence: The night type S sets the rate, so T depends on S. Given S, the arrivals form a Poisson process. Ambulances that bring several patients at once break this assumption.
method: Independent draws: S as a Bernoulli value, then T as a sum of k exponential gaps with the rate of the night. The estimators are fractions, ratios of means and a sample mean.

title: How large an A/B test before the shop launches the new checkout page?
decision: Decision: the size of the A/B test before the shop launches page B. The launch rule is P(rate B > rate A) ≥ 0.95 and an expected loss of at most 0.0001. Estimated quantity: P(rate B > rate A) and the expected loss E[max(A − B, 0)] for each test size.
reason: Each visitor converts or not, with the rate of the page. After s conversions in n visits, the uniform prior Beta(1, 1) gives the posterior law Beta(1 + s, 1 + n − s). The beta law is the conjugate prior of a binomial count.
inputs: The observed rates 4.0 % on page A and 4.6 % on page B are illustrative. Each alternative assumes that a test of its size gives these rates, so the counts are illustrative too. They are 80 and 92 conversions for 2,000 visitors on each page, 200 and 230 for 5,000, and 400 and 460 for 10,000. The loss limit 0.0001 is 0.01 percentage points of conversion rate.
dependence: None between the pages: different visitors see A and B, so the two posteriors are independent. The model assumes that the rates do not change during the test. A weekly cycle in the traffic breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of A and B, each as a ratio of gamma values. P(B > A) is the fraction of replicates with B > A, and the expected loss is the mean of max(A − B, 0). The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: The page shows no reference here: the quadrature over two concentrated posterior laws needs more work than its budget. A quadrature with a larger budget gives P(B > A) = 0.825, 0.930 and 0.982, and the expected losses 0.00061, 0.00013 and 0.000019, as checks. Other candidate models: a normal approximation of the difference of the rates, and a hierarchical prior from earlier tests.
interpretation: The 10,000 test is the smallest test that meets the launch rule. It gives P(B > A) about 0.98 and an expected loss of about 0.00002. The 5,000 test gives P(B > A) about 0.93 and an expected loss of about 0.00013, so it fails both parts of the rule. Reject the model if the conversion rate changes during the test, or if one visitor sees both pages.

title: How much buffer to plan for a task with a three-point estimate?
decision: Decision: the schedule buffer after the most likely duration of 14 days. Estimated quantity: P(the task ends after the deadline), the expected delay, and the expected cost of the buffer and the delay.
reason: PERT, the Program Evaluation and Review Technique, gives a task duration a beta law between the minimum and the maximum duration. This law has bounds, one mode at the most likely value, and a long tail toward the maximum. These properties fit a task that seldom ends early but can end much later.
inputs: The minimum 10 days, the most likely 14 days and the maximum 30 days are illustrative values. The PERT shapes are a = 1 + 4(mode − min)/(max − min) = 1.8 and b = 1 + 4(max − mode)/(max − min) = 4.2. The mean duration is (min + 4·mode + max)/6 = 16 days. A reserved day costs 1 and a late day costs 5 thousand currency units, also illustrative values.
dependence: None: the model has one task. In a project, the tasks on one path share causes of delay, so their durations are dependent. A sum of independent PERT durations then understates the spread of the project duration.
method: Independent draws of X ~ Beta(1.8, 4.2), and T = 10 + 20X days. The estimators are the fraction of late replicates and the means of the delay and the cost. The three buffers use the same streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by adaptive quadrature over the one beta variable. For the 6-day buffer, P(T > 20) = 0.142 and the expected delay is 0.30 days. Other candidate models: the triangular law on the same three points, with the larger mean 18 days, and a lognormal law with no upper bound.
interpretation: The 6-day buffer gives the least expected cost, about 7.5 thousand currency units, and its P(late) of about 0.14 meets the limit 0.2. The 2-day buffer is late with probability 0.45. The 10-day buffer is seldom late but costs about 10.1. Reject the model if past tasks of this kind often took longer than the stated maximum, because the beta law has no mass above it.

title: Which inspection policy for the lots of a supplier?
decision: Decision: the inspection policy for each lot from the supplier. A bad lot has more than 5 % defects. Estimated quantity: the expected cost of a lot, the expected number of defective units at the customer, and P(a bad lot reaches the customer).
reason: The process of the supplier drifts, so the defect fraction p differs from lot to lot. The beta law is the usual model for a fraction on [0, 1] that varies between groups. Given p, the number of defects in a random sample is binomial.
inputs: Lots of 2,000 units and a defect fraction p ~ Beta(2, 98) with mean 0.02 are illustrative values. So are the inspection cost 0.5 for each unit and the cost 20 for each defective unit at the customer. Full inspection finds and replaces each defective unit. The sample rule inspects 50 units and sends the lot to full inspection when the sample has more than 1 defect.
dependence: The defect count K depends on p: K ~ Binomial(50, p) given p. The binomial count ignores the finite lot, a small error for 50 units out of 2,000. Lots are independent. A run of bad lots after a process change breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws: first p from the beta law, then K given p. The estimators are means and fractions over the replicates. In the model, the alternative with n = 0 and c = 0 accepts every lot. The alternative with n = 0 and c = −1 sends every lot to full inspection. The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over p and a sum over the values of K. P(p > 0.05) = 0.039 is the share of bad lots. Other candidate models: a hypergeometric sample count for small lots, and a mixture of two process states in place of the beta law.
interpretation: The rule 'sample 50, accept if K ≤ 1' gives the least expected cost, about 741 for each lot. No inspection costs 800 and full inspection costs 1,000. The rule sends a bad lot to the customer with probability 0.0075, below the limit 0.01. No inspection fails the limit, with 0.039. Reject the model if the defect fractions of consecutive lots are correlated.

title: When can a news desk call a three-party race from a poll?
decision: Decision: the poll size that lets the news desk call the race for party A. The desk calls the race when P(A has the largest share) ≥ 0.95. Estimated quantity: P(A has the largest share), P(A > 50 %), and the expected cost of the poll and of a wrong call.
reason: Each respondent names one of three parties, so the poll counts are multinomial. With the uniform prior Dirichlet(1, 1, 1), the posterior law of the three vote shares is Dirichlet(1 + counts). The Dirichlet law is the conjugate prior of a multinomial count.
inputs: The poll shares 46 %, 42 % and 12 % are illustrative. Each alternative assumes that a poll of its size gives these shares, so the counts are illustrative too. An interview costs 20 and a wrong call costs 200,000 currency units, also illustrative values.
dependence: The three shares are negatively correlated, because they sum to 1. The Dirichlet law holds this dependence. The model assumes a simple random sample of voters who vote as they answer. Turnout and late changes of opinion break this assumption.
method: Independent draws of the share vector as normalised gamma values. The estimators are fractions of replicates and means. The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: The page has no quadrature for a vector law. Only the mean lead E[X1 − X2] has a reference, by linearity: (nA − nB)/(n + 3) for a poll of n, about 0.040. The marginal law Beta(1 + nA, 2 + nB + nC) of X1 gives the exact P(A > 50 %): 0.034, 0.0052, 0.00016 and 0.0000002. Other candidate models: a design effect for a cluster sample, and a model of turnout.
interpretation: The poll of 1,000 gives the least expected cost, about 38,000. But its P(A leads) of about 0.91 is below the threshold 0.95. The poll of 2,000 is the best poll that meets the threshold. It has P(A leads) of about 0.97 and a cost of about 45,600. P(A > 50 %) stays small, so the desk cannot report a majority. Reject the model if the poll misses groups of voters, because the posterior then has the wrong centre.

title: How much capacity to give the video queue of a backbone link?
decision: Decision: the capacity of the video queue at the daily peak: keep 6 Gbit/s, or upgrade to 6.5 or 7 Gbit/s. Estimated quantity: P(the video load is more than the queue capacity) on one day, the expected excess load, and the expected daily cost.
reason: The daily traffic mix is a vector of shares with the sum 1. The Dirichlet law is the usual model for random shares. Its mean gives the typical mix, and its concentration sets the change from day to day. Each share has a beta marginal law, and the shares are negatively correlated.
inputs: The total peak load of 10 Gbit/s and the concentration 40 are illustrative values. So is the mean mix: 55 % video, 25 % web, 5 % voice and 15 % backup. The upgrades cost 8 and 20 currency units a day. Each Gbit/s of video load above the capacity costs 100 currency units, also an illustrative value.
dependence: The shares of one day are dependent through their sum. The model fixes the total peak load at 10 Gbit/s and makes the days independent. A growth trend in the total load, or a week with a large sports event, breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of the share vector as normalised gamma values. The estimators are the fraction of days with an overflow and the means of the excess and the cost. The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: The page has no quadrature for a vector law, so only the mean video load 10·E[X1] = 5.5 Gbit/s has a reference, by linearity. The video share alone has the law Beta(22, 18), which gives the exact overflow probabilities 0.265, 0.100 and 0.024 for the three capacities. Other candidate models: a random total load, and a time series of the mix with dependence between days.
interpretation: The upgrade to 6.5 Gbit/s gives the least expected cost, about 11.3 a day, but it overflows on about 10 % of days. Only the upgrade to 7 Gbit/s meets the limit of 5 %, with P(overflow) about 0.024 and a cost of about 20.6 a day. Reject the model if the video share of one day predicts the share of the next day.

title: Which measure protects juvenile salmon from a river predator?
decision: Decision: the measure that protects juvenile salmon from a river predator: no measure, a seasonal deterrent, or a covered bypass channel. Estimated quantity: P(the salmon take is more than the sustainable take) and the expected cost of the measure and of the excess take.
reason: Each prey item in a stomach is one of four prey types, so the counts are multinomial. With the uniform prior Dirichlet(1, 1, 1, 1), the posterior law of the four diet shares is Dirichlet(1 + counts). The shares have the sum 1, so a larger share of salmon leaves less for the other prey.
inputs: The counts of 18 salmon, 11 sculpin, 7 crayfish and 4 other prey items are illustrative. The predators eat 20,000 prey items in a season, and the salmon run can sustain a take of 7,000 fish. Each fish above that take costs 0.02 thousand currency units. The deterrent costs 20 and removes 30 % of the salmon take. The channel costs 60 and removes 60 %. These values are illustrative.
dependence: The four shares are dependent through their sum. The model assumes that each prey item is an independent draw from the diet. The prey items of one stomach often come from one meal, so they cluster, and the posterior is then too narrow.
method: Independent draws of the share vector as normalised gamma values. The estimators are fractions of replicates and the means of the take and the cost. The diet does not depend on the measure, so P(salmon share > 0.4) is the same for each alternative. The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: The page has no quadrature for a vector law. Only the expected take has a reference, by linearity. It is 20,000·(19/44) times the fraction that the measure keeps: about 8,640, 6,050 and 3,450 fish. The salmon share alone has the law Beta(19, 25), which gives the exact P(X1 > 0.4) = 0.660. For the three measures, it gives P(take > 7,000) = 0.865, 0.180 and almost 0. Other candidate models: a Dirichlet-multinomial model with one cluster for each stomach, and diet shares that change with the season.
interpretation: The seasonal deterrent gives the least expected cost, about 22 thousand currency units. However, its P(take > 7,000) is about 0.18, above the limit 0.1. The covered channel meets the limit and costs 60. Salmon are more than 40 % of the diet with probability about 0.66, and the main prey with probability about 0.89. Reject the model if the stomach samples come from a few predators only, because the prey counts are then not independent.

title: The chi-square law is a sum of squared normal values
observe: Under the normal approximation N(ν, 2ν), each tail beyond 2 standard deviations has the probability 0.0228. The exact upper tail is about 0.050 for ν = 1, 0.045 for ν = 5 and 0.035 for ν = 30. Thus the normal approximation is poor in the tail for small ν, and it is still too small for ν = 30. The lower tail is 0 for ν = 1 and 5, because ν − 2√(2ν) is below 0, and about 0.008 for ν = 30. The page draws X as a sum of ν squared standard normal values, and the estimate of E[X] is near ν.

prob upper = X > nu + 2*sqrt(2*nu) "P(X > ν + 2√(2ν)); the normal approximation gives 0.0228"
prob lower = X < nu - 2*sqrt(2*nu) "P(X < ν − 2√(2ν)); the normal approximation gives 0.0228"
mean m = X "E[X] = ν"

alt "ν = 5": nu = 5

focus X

title: Where to set the alarm limit of an S chart for a shaft grinder?
decision: Decision: the alarm limit on the sample standard deviation S of 5 parts. Estimated quantity: for one sample, P(false alarm) in control and P(alarm) after a fault that raises σ from 20 to 30 µm.
reason: Let the part dimensions be independent and normal with standard deviation σ. Then (n − 1)S²/σ² has the chi-square law with n − 1 degrees of freedom. Thus the alarm probability of an S chart is a chi-square tail probability.
inputs: Samples of n = 5 parts, σ = 20 µm in control and σ = 30 µm after a fault are illustrative values. The alternatives are the limits 35, 37, 40 and 43 µm on S. The limit on false alarms is 0.005 for each sample, about one false alarm in 200 hours.
dependence: None: the parts of one sample are independent, and the model looks at one sample. Tool wear makes consecutive parts dependent, and the chi-square law then does not hold.
method: One chi-square variable V gives both cases: S² = σ²V/(n − 1), with σ = 20 µm or 30 µm. The estimators are the fractions of replicates with S above the limit. The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over V. They agree with the closed form P(χ²(4) > 4L²/σ²) for the limit L. E[S²] = σ² = 400 µm² has a reference by linearity. For the 40 µm limit, P(false alarm) = 0.0030 and P(alarm after a fault) = 0.130. Other candidate models: a range chart, and a chart of the exponentially weighted mean of S².
interpretation: The 40 µm limit gives the best detection, P(alarm) about 0.13 after a fault, among the limits with P(false alarm) ≤ 0.005. The 35 and 37 µm limits detect more, but they give false alarms with probability 0.016 and 0.008. Reject the model if the part dimensions have a heavier tail than the normal law, because the chi-square law then understates the false alarms.

param sigma1 = 30 {µm} "process standard deviation after a fault"

alt "Limit 35 µm": limit = 35
alt "Limit 37 µm": limit = 37
alt "Limit 40 µm": limit = 40
alt "Limit 43 µm": limit = 43

title: Which receiver class meets a 95 % position specification?
decision: Decision: the receiver class for a survey of 2,000 fixes. The specification asks for 95 % of the fixes within 5 m. Estimated quantity: P(error radius > 5 m), the mean squared error, and the expected cost of the rent and of the fixes measured again.
reason: The errors in the east, north and up directions are independent and normal, each with mean 0 and standard deviation σ. The squared error radius divided by σ² is then a sum of 3 squared standard normal values. This sum has the chi-square law with 3 degrees of freedom.
inputs: The classes with σ = 1.0, 1.5 and 2.5 m and their rents 1,200, 500 and 200 are illustrative values. So is the cost 3 of a fix measured again. The model assumes the same σ in the 3 directions. On real receivers the vertical error is larger.
dependence: None: the 3 coordinate errors are independent with equal σ, and the fixes are independent. The errors of real receivers are correlated in time, so fixes close in time fail together.
method: Independent draws of Q ~ χ²(3), and R = σ√Q. The estimators are the fraction of replicates with R > 5 m and the means of σ²Q and of the cost. The alternatives use the same streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over Q, and E[σ²Q] = 3σ² by linearity. The 95 % quantile of χ²(3) is 7.81, so the class with σ = 1.5 m puts 95 % of the fixes within 4.2 m. Other candidate models: a larger vertical σ, and a heavier tail from multipath errors.
interpretation: Class 2, with σ = 1.5 m, gives the least expected cost, about 567, and its P(R > 5 m) is about 0.011. Class 3 has the lowest rent but fails the specification with P(R > 5 m) about 0.26. Reject the model if the 3 errors have different σ or a common bias, because R²/σ² then does not have the chi-square law.

title: Which turbine model gives the most value at a windy site?
decision: Decision: the turbine model for a site with a mean wind speed of about 7 m/s. Estimated quantity: the mean power, P(no output), and the expected net value for each year.
reason: In a common model, the two horizontal components of the wind are independent normal values with mean 0 and the same σ. Then V²/σ² is a sum of 2 squared standard normal values, which has the chi-square law with 2 degrees of freedom. Thus V = σ√W has the Rayleigh law, the Weibull law with shape 2.
inputs: σ = 5.6 m/s gives the mean wind speed σ√(π/2), about 7.0 m/s. The three power curves, the annual costs 300, 480 and 420 thousand currency units and the price 60 currency units/MWh are illustrative values. The power rises as V³ from the cut-in speed to the rated speed. It stays at the rated power up to the cut-out speed, and it is 0 above that speed.
dependence: None in this model: each replicate is one independent hour of wind. Real wind speeds are correlated over hours. This does not change the means, but it changes the variance of the energy of one year.
method: Independent draws of W ~ χ²(2), and V = σ√W. The estimators are the mean power, the fraction of replicates with no output, and the mean net value. The three models use the same streams.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over W. P(V < 3 m/s) = 1 − exp(−9/(2σ²)) = 0.134 is the no-output probability of Model A, with a very small addition above 25 m/s. Other candidate models: a Weibull law fitted to the measured wind of the site, and a mean wind that changes with the season.
interpretation: Model C, the low-wind turbine, gives the largest net value, about 80 thousand currency units a year. Its mean power is about 950 kW, and it gives no output in about 10 % of hours. Model B has the largest rated power but seldom reaches it, so its net value is negative. Reject the model if the measured wind speeds do not fit a Weibull law with a shape near 2.

title: Heavy tails of Student's t law
observe: On the log survival plot, P(|T| > 4) is about 0.090 for ν = 1.5, 0.028 for ν = 3 and 0.00038 for ν = 30. title: Which outlier rule to apply to repeated length measurements?
decision: Decision: the rejection limit k, in units of the error scale s, for single measured values of a gauge block. Estimated quantity: P(the rule rejects a good value), and P(the rule keeps a value with a gross error of 4 µm).
reason: The error of one measured value is normal for a given precision. The precision changes between measurements with the temperature, the contact force and the operator. If the precision has a gamma law, the error has the t law: a scale mixture of normal laws, with heavier tails.
inputs: The block deviates by m = 0.2 µm from its nominal length. The error scale is s = 0.5 µm, with ν = 4 degrees of freedom. The rule must catch a gross error of g = 4 µm, which is 8 s. These values are illustrative. The rule compares each value with the reference value m, from the median of many values.
dependence: None: the errors of different measurements are independent. A temperature drift during one day breaks this assumption, because it moves many values together.
method: Independent draws of T. Each replicate gives one good value m + s·T and one value m + s·T + g with the gross error, from the same T. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams, so the paired differences between the limits are precise.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of T: P(|T| > k) and P(|T + 8| ≤ k). A normal model gives P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027 and P(|Z| > 4) = 0.00006. It understates the false rejections by a factor of about 15 at k = 3 and about 250 at k = 4. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a normal law with a mixture of gross errors of random size.
interpretation: k = 5 meets the limit of 1 % false rejections with the least risk to keep the gross error. P(the rule rejects a good value) is about 0.0075, and P(it keeps the gross error) about 0.020. Under the t model, k = 3 and k = 4 reject about 4.0 % and 1.6 % of good values. A normal model would accept k = 3. Reject the model if many repeated values show tails lighter than the t law, or if the values drift with time.

title: How large can a stock position be under a daily loss limit?
decision: Decision: the size of a stock position. Estimated quantity: P(the daily loss exceeds 250 thousand currency units), the expected loss beyond this limit, and the expected daily profit.
reason: The volatility of a stock changes from day to day. A normal daily return with a gamma law for its precision gives the t law. With ν = 4, the tail probability decreases as a power of the loss, as in many return series.
inputs: A mean return m = 0.0003 a day, a scale s = 0.0085 and ν = 4 are illustrative values. The standard deviation of the return is s·√2, about 1.2 % a day. The loss limit is 250 thousand currency units a day. The positions are 3, 5, 7 and 9 million currency units.
dependence: None in this model: it describes one day only. Real returns show volatility clusters, so a large loss makes the next large loss more likely. A model with a volatility that changes with time describes that.
method: Independent draws of T. The loss of the day is −V(m + s·T). The estimators are the fraction of days with a breach, and the means of the excess loss and of the profit. The alternatives share the streams, so one draw of T gives the loss of each position.
diagnostics: Reference values by quadrature over the quantile function of T for P(breach). The expected profit V·m is exact by linearity. The excess loss has no reference: the page cannot show that its moments exist, although its mean is finite for ν > 1. A normal model with the same standard deviation gives P(breach) = 0.0014 for 7 million, against 0.0066 for the t model. Other candidate models: the normal law, and a skewed t law for a market with crashes.
interpretation: 7 million is the largest position that meets the limit. Its P(breach) is about 0.0066, and its expected loss beyond the limit about 0.6 thousand currency units a day. 9 million gives P(breach) of about 0.015, above 0.01. A normal model would accept 9 million, with P(breach) = 0.0098. Reject the model if the past fraction of days beyond the limit is far from the model value, or if large losses come in clusters.

param V = 5000 {thousand currency units} "size of the position"
param m = 0.0003 "mean daily return"
param s = 0.0085 "scale of the daily return"
param nu = 4 "degrees of freedom of the return law"
param limit = 250 {thousand currency units} "daily loss limit"
T ~ student(nu = nu) "standard t value of the day"
loss := -V*(m + s*T) {thousand currency units} "loss of the day"
prob breach = loss > limit "the loss of the day exceeds the limit"

alt "5 million": V = 5000

alt "9 million": V = 9000

title: Which go threshold for a small pilot trial?
decision: Decision: the go threshold c for the t statistic of a pilot trial with 8 patients. Estimated quantity: P(go) when the treatment has no effect, and P(go) when the true effect is 0.8 standard deviations.
reason: The changes in blood pressure of the patients are independent normal values. The t statistic is the mean change divided by its standard error. With no effect, it has the t law with n − 1 = 7 degrees of freedom. This is the classical sampling law of t.
inputs: The values n = 8 patients, a true effect δ = 0.8 standard deviations and the thresholds 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 are illustrative. The limit for a false go is 0.1, a one-sided level that pilot trials often accept.
dependence: The changes of different patients are independent. The model draws T and U = Σz², the sum of squares of the standardised changes. With no effect, U has the χ²(8) law and is independent of T, because T depends only on the direction of the vector of changes.
method: Independent draws of T and U. The sum of squares about the mean is V = U/(1 + T²/7). The t statistic of the same patients with the effect is T + δ√n/√(V/7). The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
diagnostics: P(false go) = P(T > c) is an exact closed form from the t survival function, for example 0.089 at c = 1.5. P(true go) has no reference, because its quadrature over T and U exceeds the budget of the page. The noncentral t law gives 0.895, 0.776 and 0.618. A normal model of the statistic gives P(false go) = 0.067 at c = 1.5, so it understates the false go decisions. Other candidate models: the normal approximation of the statistic, and a sign test for changes that are not normal.
interpretation: c = 1.5 meets the limit of 0.1 with P(false go) of about 0.089. It gives a go for the true effect with a probability of about 0.78. c = 1.0 gives too many false go decisions, about 0.175. c = 2.0 gives a go for the true effect with a probability of only about 0.62. Reject the model if the changes are skewed or have outliers, because the t law then does not describe the statistic.

dsl:
title: Which go threshold for a small pilot trial?
problem: A pilot trial measures the change in blood pressure of 8 patients. The team starts a large trial when the t statistic exceeds a threshold. Find the threshold that limits false go decisions and keeps a good chance to detect a real effect.

param delta = 0.8 "true effect, in standard deviations of the change"
param c = 1.5 "go threshold for the t statistic"

alt "c = 1.5": c = 1.5

title: Which critical value for the fertiliser trials of a research station?
decision: Decision: the critical value c of the F test in the fertiliser trials of a research station. Estimated quantity: P(a claim) for a fertiliser with no effect, and P(a claim) for a fertiliser with a real effect.
reason: In an analysis of variance with normal plot errors, the F statistic is the ratio of 2 independent mean squares. With no treatment effect, it has the F(3, 16) law for 4 treatments on 5 plots each. A real effect gives the noncentral F law: a Poisson mixture of F laws with more numerator degrees of freedom.
inputs: A real effect has the noncentrality λ = 9, for example treatment effects of −0.9, −0.3, 0.3 and 0.9 standard deviations of the plot yield. The station accepts at most 3 false claims in 100 trials of fertilisers with no effect. These values are illustrative.
dependence: The trials of different fertilisers are independent. Inside one trial the plots are independent, with one error variance for all treatments. A soil gradient across the field breaks this assumption, and a block design then removes it.
method: Independent draws of F0 for a trial with no effect. For a trial with an effect, independent draws of J ~ Poisson(λ/2) and of F with 3 + 2J numerator degrees of freedom. The statistic F·(3 + 2J)/3 then has the noncentral F law. The estimators are fractions of replicates, and the alternatives share the streams.
diagnostics: P(F0 > c) is an exact closed form: 3.24 is the tabulated 5 % critical value, and 5.29 the 1 % value. P(a claim with an effect) has no reference, because its quadrature exceeds the budget of the page. A sum over J of F survival values gives 0.724, 0.594, 0.472 and 0.308. Other candidate models: a mixed model with random block effects, and the Kruskal–Wallis test of ranks for yields that are not normal.
interpretation: c = 4.0 detects the most real effects within the limit. P(a claim) is about 0.027 with no effect, and about 0.47 with the effect λ = 9. c = 3.24 gives about 0.050 false claims, above the limit of 0.03. If 30 % of the tested fertilisers work, about 1 claim in 9 is false at c = 4.0. Reject the model if the residuals are not normal, or if the error variance differs between treatments.

param d1 = 3 "treatment degrees of freedom: 4 treatments − 1"

title: When to switch a supplier whose parts vary more?
decision: Decision: the switch rule, which is the number of parts to compare and the critical variance ratio c. Estimated quantity: P(a needless switch) when the variances are equal, and P(a switch) when supplier 1 has 3 times the variance.
reason: For normal part dimensions, each sample variance is a scaled chi-square value, and the 2 suppliers are independent. The ratio of the sample variances then has the F(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) law when the true variances are equal. With a true variance ratio ρ, the ratio is ρ times an F value.
inputs: 13 parts from each supplier each quarter, or 26 parts each half-year, are illustrative values. So are the variance ratio ρ = 3 to detect and the limit 0.05 for a needless switch.
dependence: None: the parts are independent, and the 2 suppliers are independent. Parts from one batch can share a cause and vary less, which breaks this assumption.
method: Independent draws of F with parts − 1 degrees of freedom in the numerator and the denominator. A needless switch is the event F > c, and a switch for the ratio ρ is the event ρF > c. The estimators are fractions of replicates. The alternatives share the streams.
diagnostics: P(F > c) is an exact closed form from the incomplete beta function, and P(ρF > c) comes from quadrature. The tabulated 5 % critical values are 2.69 for F(12, 12) and 1.96 for F(25, 25). Other candidate models: Levene's test for dimensions that are not normal, and a control chart of the sample standard deviation.
interpretation: The half-year rule with c = 2 detects the larger variance with a probability of about 0.84. Its probability of a needless switch is about 0.045. The quarterly rule with c = 3 also meets the limit, but it detects with a probability of only 0.50. The quarterly rule with c = 2.5 switches without need with a probability of 0.063, above the limit. The half-year rule decides later, so a bad supplier stays longer. Reject the model if the dimensions are not normal, because the F test is sensitive to the tails.

title: How many repeats to compare the precision of 2 analysers?
decision: Decision: the number of repeats n on each analyser. Estimated quantity: P(the test rejects equal precision when it holds), P(the test accepts an analyser with 3 times the variance), and the cost.
reason: Repeated measurements of one control sample have independent normal errors. The ratio of the 2 sample variances, new over old, then has the F(n − 1, n − 1) law when the precision is equal. A new analyser with ρ times the variance gives ρ times an F value.
inputs: The limit L = 2, a worse analyser with ρ = 3 and a cost of 15 currency units for each measurement are illustrative values. The limits are 0.05 for a wrong rejection and 0.15 for a wrong acceptance.
dependence: None: the measurements are independent. A drift during the series breaks this assumption and makes the sample variance too large.
method: Independent draws of F. The estimators are the fractions of replicates with F > L and with ρF ≤ L. The cost 2·n·15 is a constant. The alternatives share the streams, but the law of F changes with n.
diagnostics: P(F > L) is an exact closed form, and P(ρF ≤ L) comes from quadrature. The cost is exact. With the tabulated 5 % critical value instead of L, for example 1.86 for F(29, 29), the wrong rejection would be 0.05 for each n. Other candidate models: errors with heavier tails than the normal law, which make the F law wrong, and Levene's test for such errors.
interpretation: 30 repeats is the least cost that meets both limits. It gives a wrong rejection of about 0.033 and a wrong acceptance of about 0.14, for 900 currency units. 20 repeats give a wrong rejection of about 0.070, above the limit. Reject the model if the measurements drift during the series, or if the errors have heavy tails.

title: Which play-off format lets the stronger team win?
decision: Decision: the format of a play-off between 2 teams: one game, best of 3 or best of 5. Estimated quantity: the probability that the stronger team wins the series, and the expected number of games played.
reason: The Elo model gives each team a performance in each game. The logistic version takes the difference of the 2 performances as logistic, with location d and scale 400/ln 10. Then P(the stronger team wins one game) = 1/(1 + 10^(−d/400)), the Elo formula.
inputs: An Elo difference d = 120 points and a target probability of 0.7 are illustrative values. Basketball has no draws, so each game has a winner. The model has no home advantage.
dependence: The games are independent, with the same law. Fatigue, injuries and home advantage make the games of a series dependent. The model ignores them.
method: Independent draws of 5 performance differences, D repeat 5. The run counts the wins after each game and the games played until one team has the wins it needs. The estimators are means over replicates. The alternatives share the streams, so the same games decide each format.
diagnostics: No reference from the page, because D repeats. Closed forms: one game gives p = 1/(1 + 10^(−0.3)), about 0.666. Best of 3 gives p²(3 − 2p), about 0.740. Best of 5 gives p³(10 − 15p + 6p²), about 0.789. The expected numbers of games are 2.445 and 3.964. Other candidate models: the normal version of the Elo model, and a model with home advantage.
interpretation: Best of 3 is the shortest format that meets the target 0.7. The stronger team wins it with a probability of about 0.740, in about 2.45 games. One game gives only 0.667. Best of 5 raises the probability to about 0.789, but it takes about 1.5 more games. Reject the model if the results of past series differ from the Elo forecast, or if home games change the results.

dsl:
title: Which play-off format lets the stronger team win?
problem: Two basketball teams with an Elo difference of 120 points meet in a play-off. A longer series makes a win of the stronger team more likely, but it takes more games. Find the shortest format that the stronger team wins with a probability of at least 0.7.
param d = 120 {Elo points} "Elo difference of the 2 teams"
param sc = 400/log(10) {Elo points} "logistic scale of the performance difference"
param games = 3 {games} "length of the series: 1, 3 or 5"
param need = (games + 1)/2 {games} "wins needed to take the series"
D ~ logistic(mu = d, s = sc) repeat 5 {Elo points} "performance difference in each game"
w1 := D[1] > 0 {games} "wins of the stronger team after game 1"
w2 := w1 + (D[2] > 0) {games} "wins after game 2"
w3 := w2 + (D[3] > 0) {games} "wins after game 3"
w4 := w3 + (D[4] > 0) {games} "wins after game 4"
w5 := w4 + (D[5] > 0) {games} "wins after game 5"

alt "Best of 5": games = 5
